catalog_quote: Stress in Central Lembata is marked by increased vowel length and higher pitch. In unstressed syllables, vowels can be reduced to schwa. In Central Lembata, the penultimate syllable of the word is stressed, unless the penultimate contains the vowel schwa. This becomes clear in suffixed nouns, such as kopong /ˈko.poŋ/ 'child' → kopong-u /ko.ˈpo.ŋu/ 'child-spec', which are both stressed on the penultimate syllable. ... However, in trisyllabic stems with final sequences of two identical vowels, the surface realisation shows ultimate stress, as in /tu.ˈlu.u/ 'repair' which is realised as [tuˈluː]. ... Schwa is the only penultimate vowel that cannot be stressed. Words with penultimate schwa are stressed at the ultimate syllable, such as /bə.ˈka/ 'to fly'. new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Central Lembata (catalog-all-2026-09-12) with an EMPTY rule and there are no existing statements, so this fills the gap rather than agreeing or contradicting: penultimate stress with a schwa-skipping exception and a weight-driven tendency toward heavy CVC final syllables. Describes the variety of the Central Lembata highlands (Fricke's own fieldwork; the same variety as the 2017 Wacana article).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (longer vowel, higher pitch) falls on the penultimate syllable of the morphosyntactic word, including after suffixation (kopong → kopong-u both penult). Schwa cannot be stressed: a penultimate schwa shifts stress to the final syllable (even if that is also schwa). Underlyingly trisyllabic stems ending in two identical vowels (/tu.ˈlu.u/ → [tu.ˈluː]) surface with final stress and long vowel, giving surface minimal pairs by length/stress (ex. 6). Consonant-final words vary between penult and final stress ([ˈke.dak] ~ [ke.ˈdak]), explained as a competing tendency to stress heavy CVC final syllables; an epenthetic final schwa ([ke.ˈda.kə]) restores penultimate stress. Author's summary (p. 50): 'Central Lembata words have penultimate stress, unless the penultimate is a schwa.' Appendix A.1 (p. 425): stress is not marked in phonemic transcriptions 'because stress in Central Lembata is not always stable (cf. §3.2.5)'.
new_statements.exceptions: Penultimate schwa -> ultimate stress; final identical-vowel sequences -> surface ultimate stress with long vowel; consonant-final words show free variation penult ~ ultimate (tendency to stress heavy CVC finals), repaired by schwa epenthesis; a few disyllabic clitic-like markers (bo, ro) are monosyllabic CV.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe Central Lembata Lamaholot, the variety of the central mountains of Lembata island (Fricke's fieldwork), distinct from the coastal Lamaholot varieties described earlier. The 2019 dissertation's Chapter 3 'A grammar of Central Lembata' is the source read.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every quoted string in the record is verbatim in the LOT 544 PDF we hold at book pp. 49-50 = pp. 73-74, sec. 3.2.5-3.2.6, exactly as the locator says. (2) Deciding source: Fricke 2019 is a Leiden dissertation whose Part I is a full fieldwork grammar of Central Lembata; it is the only description of this language's phonology in existence (Glottolog has one descriptive ref, also by Fricke, on nouns/pronouns; Crossref shows no other author working on the language).
